solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Leave empty venue in which a mouser resides (6)

indicatorNotes.empty: an emptied word has had its contents scooped out, leaving only its outside letters
indicatorNotes.in which: points back to the shell of venue as the place where the next piece goes
indicatorNotes.resides: the mouser lives inside that shell, so its letters sit within it

blocks.note: a mouser = a cat, kept for catching mice

annotation.surface: A cat has moved into a deserted hall and somebody wants to clear out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leave empty' looks like one instruction to clear the hall, but 'Leave' alone is the definition and 'empty' works on venue.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: tenants who move out of a flat or guests quitting a hotel room are departing from it.

entries.clue: Certainly in the pink (4,4)

blocks.note: a reply agreeing to a request
an idiom for being in fine health

annotation.surface: Someone confirms they are in excellent health.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: as a reply agreeing to something, and as a report on how you feel.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday: saying yes to a request, and describing someone in excellent health.

entries.clue: Have little effect – as would blunted skate? (3,2,3)

blocks.note: an idiom for failing to impress or persuade
a blade with no edge would glide without scoring the rink

annotation.surface: A skater grumbles that dull blades get them nowhere.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half takes the idiom literally; the question mark flags that playful reading.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: an argument that makes no impression on the listener, like a blunt blade on a frozen pond.

entries.clue: Before winner at the death, draw level (4)

indicatorNotes.Before: the draw's letters are placed ahead of the winner's letter
indicatorNotes.at the death: sporting slang for the final moments of a match, so the final letter

blocks.note: a drawn match is a tie

annotation.surface: A team equalises just before a late winning goal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Draw level' reads as one sporting phrase, but 'level' is the definition and 'draw' belongs to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: stadium seating, wedding cakes and organisations are built in stacked layers.

entries.clue: Demonstration of arrogance in song a bit misplaced (8)

indicatorNotes.misplaced: letters put in the wrong places have to be rearranged into the right ones

annotation.surface: A singer's arrogance shows in a slightly off-key number.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A bit misplaced' looks like a mild criticism of the song; 'a bit' is fodder and only 'misplaced' does the work.
annotation.definitionFit: Bragging loudly about your own achievements is the most obvious way pride shows itself.

entries.clue: Just around the corner – as is setting sun? (2,3,7)

blocks.note: where the sun sits at dusk, on the line between earth and sky

annotation.surface: Someone at dusk says the end of the day is near.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half takes the phrase literally, which the question mark signals.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for something imminent, borrowed from a ship or storm first seen far off where sky meets land.

entries.clue: Fielder in error? (4)

blocks.note: a cricket position close behind the batter, beside the wicketkeeper
a small careless mistake, a lapse

annotation.surface: A cricket fielder has dropped a catch.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket, the slips are fielders stationed close behind the batter, beside the wicketkeeper.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a cricket position waiting for edged catches, and a small careless mistake.

entries.clue: Bunch of flowers one takes off (6)

blocks.note: a plane taking off goes up

annotation.surface: A florist removes a bunch of blooms from display.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Takes off' tempts as removal; here it is lift-off, as an aircraft climbs.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a plural is needed because a bunch holds several stems of these purple garden blooms.

entries.clue: Player in concert, leader of orchestra, look! (6)

indicatorNotes.leader of: whatever leads a word is at its front, so the opening letter

blocks.note: lo = look, as in 'lo and behold'

annotation.surface: A musician performing at a concert, with the orchestra's leader in view.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Player' looks musical in a clue about an orchestra, but it means a womaniser.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang sense: a man who plays the field, kept by wealthy women for romance, is a player in that sense.

entries.clue: Quite hot after temperature in back turns (6)

indicatorNotes.in: the temperature-and-hot pair goes inside the reversed back
indicatorNotes.turns: the word for back turns round, reading right to left

annotation.surface: Someone notices the heat creeping back as the weather turns.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quite hot' reads as one phrase about the weather; 'Quite' alone is the definition and 'hot' is just a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both soften an adjective, as in a fairly good film.

entries.clue: Remarkable man joins band, shortly (8)

indicatorNotes.joins: the man is attached to the end of the band's letters
indicatorNotes.shortly: in brief form, so the word is cut short by a letter

blocks.note: a king is a chess man

annotation.surface: A notable musician is about to join a group.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' reads as a group of musicians; it is a strip. 'Man' is a chess piece, here the king.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something eye-catching and impressive enough to draw attention and comment.

entries.clue: Unfortunately, free agents do procrastinate (4,4,4)

indicatorNotes.Unfortunately: things going badly for the letters means they end up disordered

annotation.surface: A grumble that people left to themselves always put things off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like a link, but it is fodder: the three words together supply all twelve letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone reluctant to move walks slowly, scuffing along, so it means delaying deliberately.

entries.clue: Logs cut, fine bark (4)

indicatorNotes.cut: a word that is cut loses a piece, here its final letter

annotation.surface: Firewood chopped, and the tree's rough bark is fine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bark' sits by logs as the tree's skin, but it is the dog's.
annotation.definitionFit: The sound a dog makes, written as a word in comics and children's books.

entries.clue: Groom up for marriage, bride uncertain, all ending (5)

indicatorNotes.all ending: every word contributes the letter at its end

blocks.note: last letters of uP foR marriagE bridE uncertaiN

annotation.surface: A groom ready to wed while the bride has doubts, and everything ending.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Groom' pretends to be the bridegroom; it is the verb, to tidy oneself.
annotation.definitionFit: Birds smooth their feathers with their beaks, and people fussing over their appearance do the same.

entries.clue: Stagger as if drunk, gaze when falling back (4)

indicatorNotes.falling back: a retreating word goes backwards, so read its letters right to left

blocks.note: to leer is to gaze lewdly

annotation.surface: A drunk stares blearily and then topples backwards.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Falling back' looks like part of the drunk's stagger; it tells you to turn the gaze round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to lurch and sway unsteadily, as after a blow or too much wine.

entries.clue: Sign initial on banknotes in Turkish currency (5)

indicatorNotes.initial: the initial of a word is its opening letter
indicatorNotes.in: that letter goes inside the currency's name

annotation.surface: Someone initials Turkish banknotes before signing off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sign' pretends to be the verb for initialling notes; it is a zodiac sign.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the scales are one of the twelve star signs of the zodiac.

entries.clue: From hiding place, shoot bird (5)

blocks.note: to fire from cover at a target

annotation.surface: A hunter fires at a bird from a hide.
annotation.walkthrough: The verb comes from the bird: it was so hard to hit that marksmen good enough were called snipers.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a marsh wader with a long beak, and firing at people from concealment.

entries.clue: Coming together, instruments clashing (7,5)

annotation.surface: An orchestra's instruments join in a jarring discord.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clashing' sounds like discordant music; it means fighting, like stags with antlers locked.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from rutting stags, whose antlers catch together as they fight, used for people in open conflict.

entries.clue: South American in rave-up, dancing (8)

indicatorNotes.dancing: dancers move about the floor, so the letters move into a new order

annotation.surface: A South American is dancing at a lively party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link, but it supplies two of the fodder letters. A rave-up is a wild party.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a native of Lima or the Andes belongs to one country on that continent.

entries.clue: Plane is not broken up for scrap (8)

indicatorNotes.broken up: something smashed into bits can be reassembled differently, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: An aircraft is intact and so is not being broken up for scrap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broken up for scrap' reads as one phrase about an old plane; 'scrap' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Originally throwing cargo overboard to lighten a ship, now discarding any plan or thing.

entries.clue: Is man on battlefield drawing on literary work? (12)

indicatorNotes.on: one thing placed on another follows it here, so the battlefield comes first

blocks.note: the front is where battle is fought
a chess man is a piece

annotation.surface: A soldier at war sketches while drawing on his reading.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drawing on' pretends to mean 'using'; 'drawing' is a picture and the whole phrase is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The illustration printed facing a book's title page, a picture placed at the front of a volume.

entries.clue: Next post filled by company (6)

indicatorNotes.filled by: something filled has another thing put inside it, so company goes in

blocks.note: to post a letter is to send it

annotation.surface: A job vacancy about to be filled by a firm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Post' looks like a job; it is the verb, to dispatch a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: following immediately in order, as the runner-up after the winner.

entries.clue: Correct site working (4-2)

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working

annotation.surface: Someone fixes a website so it works again.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Correct' reads as a verb, to fix; it is the adjective. The answer is British slang.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for exactly right, as a dart landing precisely on its target point.

entries.clue: Show hosted by Essex politician (4)

indicatorNotes.hosted by: a host holds guests within, so the answer is held inside the next words

annotation.surface: A trade fair is staged by a local MP in Essex.
annotation.walkthrough: Essex is a county east of London; here its letters matter only for the hidden run.
annotation.definitionFit: Short for exposition: a large public exhibition, such as a world's fair or trade fair.

entries.clue: Dundonian, for example, backs a Home Counties town (5)

indicatorNotes.backs: something that backs another stands behind it, so it comes after

blocks.note: someone from Dundee, a city in Scotland

annotation.surface: A Scotsman supports an English commuter town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backs' reads as supports; here it puts the Scotsman behind A. The Home Counties are the counties around London.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a Berkshire town famous for its royal racecourse, in a county bordering London.

entries.clue: Bet placed, nothing originally pocketed … (4)

indicatorNotes.originally: what a word is at its origin is its opening letter
indicatorNotes.pocketed: something pocketed is tucked inside, so the letter goes within placed

annotation.surface: A gambler places a bet and wins nothing, continuing in the next clue.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to 28 across; it plays no part in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for a gamble or wager, especially a speculative one at the bookmaker's.

entries.clue: Picture in bedroom lifted up (4)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer lies inside the following words
indicatorNotes.lifted up: in a down entry, lifting letters reads them bottom to top

annotation.surface: A painting in the bedroom has been hung higher.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' does double duty: its letters are in the hidden run, and it is part of the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A movie is a motion picture, and people still say they are going to the pictures.

entries.clue: Head of mammoth in particular on a mammoth! (4)

indicatorNotes.Head of: the head of a word is its top, which in a down entry is the opening letter
indicatorNotes.on: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it

annotation.surface: Someone points out the head of a woolly mammoth.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter uses 'mammoth' twice on purpose: first as the animal whose initial is used, then as the adjective meaning huge.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang for enormous, from the Greek for great, as in a blockbuster success.

entries.clue: … and I bet differently after nothing acquired! (8)

indicatorNotes.differently: arranged in a different way, so the letters are reordered
indicatorNotes.after: the rearranged letters follow the letter for nothing

annotation.surface: Continuing from 25 across: the gambler bets another way after winning nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening ellipsis only continues the story from 25 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: got hold of, gained possession of, as winnings are collected after a successful bet.

entries.clue: Einstein I observed in rank below family (6)

indicatorNotes.observed in: the letter is seen within the rank's name, so it goes inside

blocks.note: in biology, genus is the rank below family

annotation.surface: Einstein studying biological classification.
annotation.walkthrough: In taxonomy the ranks run family, then genus, then species.
annotation.definitionFit: The physicist's name is used as a common noun for anyone of exceptional intellect.

entries.clue: Terrific explosive (8)

annotation.surface: Praise for something thrilling.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words read as one phrase, but each is a separate definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: Nobel's blasting stick, and slang praise for something sensational.

entries.clue: Rule about ammunition ultimately for big gun (6)

indicatorNotes.about: the rule goes round the other letter, surrounding it
indicatorNotes.ultimately: what comes in the end, so the final letter of the word

blocks.note: a canon is a rule or law

annotation.surface: A regulation governing the supply of shells for heavy artillery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Big gun' can mean an important person; here it is the weapon.
annotation.definitionFit: A heavy artillery piece firing iron balls, as on old warships and castle walls.
